summary: Tests for the Simulation Center endpoints in `iip/routes/simulation.py`. Every scenario is generated by `iip/seed.py` and pushed through the real `process_event` pipeline, so these tests double as end-to-end detection checks: the right signals fire, related events correlate into one incident, and benign activity stays quiet. They also cover the endpoint guards, the live-traffic toggle and the demo reset.

notes.text: Docstring: scenarios use the same pipeline as real ingestion, so a passing scenario proves the whole chain (normalize, enrich, score, correlate) works together.
pytest, for `parametrize` and the custom `fresh` fixture.
The shared API-key header from `conftest.py`. Running a scenario, toggling traffic and resetting are all writes, so they need it.
The scenario catalog, a dict keyed by names such as `brute_force`. Importing it means the tests always cover every scenario that exists.
`list(SCENARIOS)` gives the scenario keys, so the next test runs once per scenario (10 today) and a newly added scenario is tested automatically.
Runs the scenario against a customer the route picks itself, authenticated with the API key.
The endpoint answers 200 OK (it sets no custom status code) and the body is parsed as JSON.
The response narrates the pipeline as six steps in a fixed order. The Simulation Center page lights up each stage by these keys, so their names and order are part of the contract.
At least one event was produced, and `top_event` really is the highest-scoring one, as the route promises.
A custom fixture that tests request by name. It returns nothing; it exists only for its side effect.

Docstring giving the reason: the earlier scenario runs hit random customers and left fresh events behind (new devices, foreign sign-ins, open incidents) that could change how the next scenario is scored.
Calls the reset endpoint, which wipes the database and re-seeds it with the fixed random seed (42), so each detection test starts from the same reproducible history.
Runs `normal_login`: one sign-in from home, on a trusted device, with a clean IP. For benign scenarios the route prefers a settled customer, one last seen at home and quiet for the past nine hours.
No incident may open and the event must be LOW. This guards against false positives: ordinary activity must never alarm analysts.
Runs `business_trip`: a sign-in at home, then a sign-in and a small payment in another city eight hours later.
A set comprehension gathers every signal raised by any event in the scenario.
A realistic flight must never be called impossible travel and must not open an incident. It is the false-positive counterpart of `test_impossible_travel_is_flagged`.
Targets a specific customer through the `user_id` query parameter, so the outcome doesn't depend on random selection.
The response confirms the scenario ran against the requested customer.

The five failed logins must be correlated into one incident holding at least five events, not five separate incidents. The first event scores HIGH and opens the incident; the later ones score at least 30 and join it.
Runs `impossible_travel` for the same fixed customer: a sign-in at home, then one from a distant foreign city (at least 1,500 km away) 20 minutes later.
The foreign sign-in must be the top event and carry the `Impossible travel` signal.
The stored travel context must show a speed above 900 km/h (the airliner limit, `rules.IMPOSSIBLE_SPEED_KMH`), proving the verdict came from the distance and speed calculation.
Targeting a customer who doesn't exist (`USR-0000`) must return 404 instead of silently picking someone else.
Runs `password_spray`, the only multi-account scenario: one flagged IP fails against the chosen customer plus five others.
The response lists every account touched; at least five must be affected.

At least one event must be flagged `Password spray`, which happens once five distinct accounts have failed from the same IP within 30 minutes. This test doesn't need `fresh`: the scenario reaches the threshold on its own, and older events could only add to the count.
Checks the endpoint's defensive behaviour.
An unknown scenario name returns 404; the route checks the name against `SCENARIOS`.
Running a scenario without the API key returns 401. Scenarios write real events, so they are protected exactly like ingestion.
The catalog endpoint lists exactly the scenarios that exist.
The live-traffic generator is off until someone switches it on, so no background events interfere with the tests.
Exercises starting and stopping the background traffic generator.

Switching traffic on reports `enabled` as true. This POST also proves `/simulation/traffic` reaches the toggle endpoint instead of being captured by `POST /simulation/{scenario}` as a scenario called traffic, which is why the route file declares static paths first.
Switching it off cancels the background task and reports `enabled` as false, so the generator can't keep inserting events while later tests run.
The reset endpoint wipes the database, re-seeds it and reports `status` as reset.
Afterwards the customer base is back to exactly 25, proving the re-seed finished (the endpoint runs it in a worker thread and waits for it before answering).
